title: Linked Lists
summary: Building a singly linked list from nodes - adding at the front and back with a tail reference, getting by index, removing, reversing in place, iterating with Iterator, the edge cases of empty and one-element lists, doubly linked lists and sentinel nodes, and comparing linked lists with array lists.

cards.q: Why is `get(i)` O(n) for a linked list?
cards.a:
There is no index: it must follow `i` links from the head

Nodes are not stored next to each other, so the only way to item `i` is to follow `next` links one at a time.

cards.q: Besides a node in the middle, which cases must `remove` handle?
cards.a:
The head, the tail, a one-node list, and a value that is not there

Most linked-list bugs live at the edges: the head has no predecessor, the tail reference must move back, and a missing value must leave the list untouched.

cards.q: In the `reverse` method, what would happen without `Node<T> next = cur.next;` at the start of the loop?
cards.a:
The rest of the list would be lost after `cur.next = prev`

The original next link must be saved before it is overwritten; otherwise there is no way to reach the following node.
